title: Evaluating Gong alternatives? Start with the workflow you need to change
summary: A practical evaluation guide for conversation intelligence, coaching and sales execution. Compare real workflows, integration depth and proof.
body_markdown:
The right Gong alternative depends on what you need to replace: conversation capture, coaching, forecasting, engagement or the work a rep does after a meeting. Write down that job before comparing feature grids.


Gong's current platform spans a revenue data foundation, AI capabilities and applications across revenue workflows. Treating it as only a call recorder produces a misleading comparison. Check the capabilities and packaging relevant to your team in its current documentation and demonstration.[Gong platform](https://www.gong.io/platform) .


This guide offers an evaluation process rather than an unsupported ranking of vendors. Cedar is one option to evaluate when the problem centers on connecting sales context with agent-assisted work. Whether it replaces or complements an existing platform depends on the workflow.


## Define the replacement boundary


List the systems that currently handle recording, CRM, email, coaching, forecasting and task execution. Then mark which systems you want to keep.


A team might be happy with its recorder but unhappy with copying notes into a CRM. Another may need manager coaching across a large team. A third may care about preparing follow-ups in the rep's existing inbox. Those are different buying decisions.


Describe the current friction as an observable sequence: “After a call, the rep opens the transcript, copies commitments into a document, updates three CRM fields and writes a follow-up.” That is more useful than “we need better AI.”


## Run the same scenario in every demonstration


Use a representative, permitted sample account with a meeting, an email exchange, a changed close date and an unresolved buyer requirement. Ask each vendor to complete the same tasks:


1. Explain the account situation and cite the evidence.
2. Identify what the rep promised.
3. Prepare the next action in the appropriate destination.
4. Propose a CRM change and show the review process.
5. Explain what happens after a buyer replies.
6. Show how a manager changes the relevant playbook.


Record what was done live, what required configuration and what was described as future functionality. A polished canned demo is not evidence that the workflow works in your environment.


## Compare the dimensions that change daily work


Dimension Question to test Evidence to request


Context Which relevant conversations can it actually access? Source-level account timeline


Grounding Can a rep inspect why a recommendation was made? Links or excerpts tied to the claim


Execution Does the work arrive where the rep can use it? Actual draft, task or CRM proposal


Control Can permissions differ by action or field? Configuration and approval behavior


Adaptation How are team rules and personal preferences applied? A live instruction change and rerun


Management Can leaders inspect behaviors and outcomes separately? Definitions, denominators and sample report


Reliability What happens when a source is missing or stale? Failure and recovery behavior


Do not infer integration depth from a logo. Reading a CRM, writing deal fields and creating new records are distinct capabilities. Likewise, receiving Slack notifications is different from reviewing and executing work in Slack.


## Test the uncomfortable cases


Include a meeting with no next step, a buyer who changes timing, an email in the wrong thread and a CRM field that conflicts with a recent call. The system should expose uncertainty instead of confidently completing the wrong action.


Ask what happens when an employee leaves, an integration disconnects or the team changes its sales stages. Request an explanation of the relevant access controls and administrative responsibilities. Evaluate the controls your organization actually needs.


A tool that performs well on clean examples can still create review work when real account data is inconsistent.


## Evaluate adoption without assuming a full replacement


Consider three options: keep the existing system and improve configuration, add a complementary workflow, or replace a defined part of the stack.


For Cedar, test the specific agent workflow and its outputs alongside your existing CRM, email and meeting tools. For Gong, test the current applications and integrations that address the same requirement. Overlap is possible; the question is whether the resulting process is better for your team.


Compare review effort and workflow completion, not just the number of generated summaries.


## Build a pilot scorecard


Before the pilot, define eligible accounts, participating reps, review period and success criteria. Measure baseline effort and error rates using the same definitions you will use afterward.


A practical scorecard might include time to a reviewable follow-up, factual corrections per draft, CRM changes accepted or rejected, missed commitments and weekly active use of the target workflow. Add revenue outcomes only when the sample and sales-cycle length support them.


Keep procurement facts separate from product judgments. Confirm current pricing, minimum commitments, included applications and implementation requirements directly with each vendor. Historical customer anecdotes are not reliable price lists.


## Make the decision from observed work


At the end, summarize which workflows passed, which need configuration, which remain unsupported and what the team would stop doing manually. Include the costs and responsibilities of running the selected approach.


A good comparison should make it easy to choose another product when it better fits the requirement. That is more useful than a table where the author wins every row.
